claim: Backtesting uniform national swing (UNS) and proportional swing against UK general elections 1997, 2001 and 2005 found no consistent superiority of either method: UNS was more accurate in 2005, proportional slightly more accurate in 2001, and the two were tied in 1997.
stance_target: proportional swing is more accurate than uniform swing
scope_conditions: UK general elections 1997, 2001, 2005; two-party swing vs seat totals
quoted_support: There is no evidence from this data that proportional swing calculations are superior to uniform swing calculations.

claim: Even the better of the two simple swing methods carries substantial national-level error: average error in predicted parliamentary majority size exceeds 30 seats.
stance_target: simple swing methods have material forecasting error even at the national aggregate level
quoted_support: On average, the majority predicted by UNS is out by over 30 seats, though there is no consistent pattern to the error.

claim: The Butler & Kavanagh study of the 1979 UK general election concluded uniform swing outperformed proportional swing at predicting that and previous elections, an early empirical precedent for UNS dominance.
stance_target: uniform swing has historically outperformed proportional swing in the UK
scope_conditions: UK general election 1979 and preceding elections
quoted_support: the Butler & Kavanagh book on the 1979 general election, The British General Election of 1979, concludes that uniform swing was superior at predicting results in that election than proportional swing and had also been at previous general elections.
